questions.prompt: How do Koch and colleagues define a neural correlate of consciousness (NCC) for a specific experience?

options.text: The minimal set of neural events and mechanisms jointly sufficient for that specific conscious experience
Any brain activity recorded while the person is awake
options.why_wrong: Much waking activity is unconscious; the NCC is the minimal sufficient part.

options.text: The single brain region where all experiences are stored
options.why_wrong: The definition concerns sufficient mechanisms, not a storage site.

options.text: Brain activity that occurs only during dreaming
options.why_wrong: NCCs are sought for experiences in general, awake or dreaming.

questions.explanation: The definition picks out the minimal neural mechanisms that together suffice for a particular experience, which separates the correlates from mere background conditions such as blood flow or arousal.

sources.citation: Koch, C., Massimini, M., Boly, M., & Tononi, G. (2016). Neural correlates of consciousness: progress and problems. Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 17, 307-321.

questions.prompt: In the contrastive method for studying consciousness, what two kinds of conditions are compared?
questions.answer_text: Conditions where the stimulus stays the same but conscious perception differs (seen versus unseen), for example in masking or binocular rivalry.
questions.explanation: Holding the input constant while experience changes lets researchers separate neural activity linked to consciousness from activity linked to the stimulus itself. Baars called this contrastive analysis.

sources.citation: Baars, B. J. (1988). A Cognitive Theory of Consciousness. Cambridge University Press.
Koch, C., Massimini, M., Boly, M., & Tononi, G. (2016). Neural correlates of consciousness: progress and problems. Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 17, 307-321.

questions.prompt: In binocular rivalry, each eye is shown a different image. What changes over time while the stimulus stays the same?

options.text: Which of the two images the person consciously sees
The images presented to each eye
options.why_wrong: The images are held constant; that is what makes rivalry useful.
The physical stimulus does not change.

questions.explanation: Perception alternates between the two images even though the input is constant, so rivalry dissociates conscious perception from the stimulus.

sources.citation: Blake, R., & Logothetis, N. K. (2002). Visual competition. Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 3, 13-21.
Koch, C., Massimini, M., Boly, M., & Tononi, G. (2016). Neural correlates of consciousness: progress and problems. Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 17, 307-321.
